system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2205-12-22 13:47:00 to 2205-12-27 14:22:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis and neurogenic bladder with a chronic suprapubic catheter, was admitted for lethargy and found to have severe sepsis from a multidrug-resistant urinary tract infection. Blood and urine cultures grew MDR E. coli and VRE, prompting treatment with daptomycin and meropenem. Imaging revealed an obstructing right kidney stone causing hydronephrosis, requiring percutaneous nephrostomy. He also developed aspiration pneumonia, likely due to impaired swallowing, and was managed with NG tube feeding before passing a swallow study and resuming a pureed diet. An ostomy prolapse was noted but managed conservatively. His condition improved with treatment, renal function normalized, and he was discharged home on a four-week course of IV antibiotics via PICC line, with follow-up planned for stone removal and surgical evaluation.
problems: Septicemia due to escherichia coli [E. coli]
Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomitus

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  History: ___ with hypoxia, pls eval for pna  //

TECHNIQUE:  Chest PA and lateral

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph ___

FINDINGS: 

Previously seen multifocal opacities in bilateral lungs have resolved since
___.  No focal consolidation suggestive of pneumonia is identified. 
Linear opacity at lateral left lung base is likely atelectasis.  5 mm ovoid
opacity at the right lung base is stable.  There is no pneumothorax or large
pleural effusion.  Cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal size.  An apparent
___ scar pericardium is an artifact as the patient went on to have a CT
urogram which include the heart and does not demonstrate a pneumopericardium. 
Cervical spine hardware is again noted.

IMPRESSION: 

No radiographic evidence of pneumonia.

EXAMINATION:  CTU (ABD/PEL) W/O CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ with likelky urosepsis, h/o obstructing stones, right
percutaneous nephrostomy tube, evaluate for location of tube, obstructing
stones.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector CT images of the abdomen and pelvis were acquired
without intravenous contrast. Non-contrast scan has several limitations in
detecting vascular and parenchymal organ abnormalities, including tumor
detection.  Note, patient unable to lie prone.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and reviewed on PACS.
Oral contrast was not administered.

DOSE:  Total DLP (Body) = 881 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast ___.

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST: Scattered streaky opacities at the lung bases are compatible with
subsegmental atelectasis; otherwise, the partially imaged lung bases are
clear. There is no pleural or pericardial effusion. There is no hiatus hernia.

CT ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY: The liver demonstrates a normal homogeneous noncontrast
appearance without apparent focal lesion.  There is no obvious intrahepatic
biliary ductal dilation.  Lack of IV contrast precludes evaluation of the
portal vein.  The gallbladder demonstrates a normal noncontrast appearance
without evidence of surrounding inflammation or radiopaque stones.  There is
no extrahepatic biliary ductal dilation.

PANCREAS: The pancreas is normal in appearance.  There is no peripancreatic
stranding or ductal dilation.

SPLEEN: A 14 mm accessory spleen is seen superiorly.  There is no
splenomegaly.

ADRENALS: The adrenal glands are normal.

URINARY: New since CT performed ___ is mild to moderate left
hydroureteronephrosis.  A dilated left ureter extends to the left UVJ, where a
0.8 cm left UVJ calculus is presumably obstructing.  At least two additional
nonobstructing stones are seen within the bladder lumen measuring 1.1 and 0.5
cm.

A right percutaneous nephrostomy tube is seen in grossly appropriate location.
There is no evidence of kinking or abnormality along the course of the tube,
which exits via the right flank.  Multiple foci of clustered nonobstructing
right renal calculi are relatively unchanged in comparison to prior CT,
measuring 0.9 (series 2, image 30) and 1.2 cm (series 2, image 40).  There is
no right hydronephrosis.

Multiple nonobstructing 0.2-0.3 cm left renal calculi are seen (for example
see series 2, image 34).

The renal parenchyma demonstrates an unremarkable noncontrast appearance
bilaterally

GASTROINTESTINAL: The stomach and duodenum are unremarkable.  A single
prominent, distended loop of small bowel measuring up to 2.8 cm, otherwise,
there is no evidence of obstruction, wall thickening, or other small bowel
abnormality.  The patient is status post sigmoid resection with a right lower
quadrant end-colostomy.  The rectal stump is unremarkable.  The colostomy site
is normal in appearance.  The colon is filled with stool, and otherwise
unremarkable.

VASCULAR AND LYMPH NODES: Mildly prominent left periaortic retroperitoneal
lymph nodes measure up to 8 mm in short axis, not pathologically enlarged by
CT size criteria, likely reactive in nature.  There is no mesenteric
lymphadenopathy.  There is no free intraperitoneal air or fluid.

CT PELVIS:
A suprapubic tube is seen entering the bladder via the right anterior abdomen,
as on prior.  Mild diffuse bladder wall thickening may relate at least
partially to underdistention, possibly in addition to a component of chronic
inflammation, overall unchanged appearance since ___.  Multiple small
intraluminal foci of gas layering anti dependently within the bladder lumen
are not unexpected in the setting of catheterization.  The distal right ureter
is unremarkable.  There is no pelvic sidewall, iliac chain, or inguinal
lymphadenopathy.  There is no free pelvic fluid.

MUSCULOSKELETAL: There is diffuse osseous demineralization.  There is moderate
dextroscoliosis centered at L1.  No concerning focal lytic or sclerotic
osseous lesions are identified.

IMPRESSION:


1. 0.8 cm obstructing left UVJ calculus resulting in new mild to moderate left
hydroureteronephrosis.
2. Multiple bilateral, right greater than left nonobstructing renal calculi
measuring up to 1.2 cm.
3. At least 2 additional nonobstructing bladder calculi, measuring up to 1.1
cm.
4. Appropriately positioned and normal-appearing right nephrostomy catheter.
5. Status post sigmoid resection with end colostomy the right lower quadrant. 
Unremarkable rectal stump.
6. Unchanged diffuse mild bladder wall thickening with small intraluminal foci
of gas, not unexpected in the setting of suprapubic catheterization.

NOTIFICATION:  The findings were discussed by Dr. ___ with Dr. ___ on
the telephone on ___ at 12:13 ___, 15 minutes after discovery of the
findings.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with urosepsis and left UVJ stone, obstructing //
PLease place L PCN

COMPARISON:  CTU from same date.

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ and Dr.
___ radiologist performed the procedure. Dr. ___
___ supervised the trainee during the key components of the procedure
and has reviewed and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
100 mcg of fentanyl and 2 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 47 min during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS:  Cefalexin 1 g IV
CONTRAST: 15 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 2.09 min, 5 mGy

PROCEDURE:  1. Left ultrasound guided renal collecting system access.
2. Left nephrostogram.
3. Percutaneous nephrostomy tube placement.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
prone on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The left flank was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

After the injection of 5 cc of 1% lidocaine in the subcutaneous soft tissues,
the left renal collecting system was accessed through a posterior lower pole
calyx under ultrasound guidance using a 21 gauge Cook needle. Ultrasound
images of the access were stored on PACS. Prompt return of urine confirmed
appropriate positioning.  Under fluoroscopic guidance, a Nitinol wire was
advanced into the renal collecting system. After a skin ___, the needle was
exchanged for an Accustick sheath. Once the tip of the sheath was in the
collecting system; the sheath was advanced over the wire, inner dilator and
metallic stiffener. The wire and inner dilator were then removed and diluted
contrast was injected into the collecting system to confirm position. An
Amplatz wire was advanced through the sheath and coiled in the collecting
system. The sheath was then removed and an 8 ___ nephrostomy tube was
advanced into the renal collecting system. The wire was then removed and the
pigtail was formed in the collecting system. Contrast injection confirmed
appropriate positioning. The catheter was then flushed, 0 silk stay sutures
applied and the catheter was secured witha Stat Lock device and sterile
dressings. The catheter was attached to a bag.

FINDINGS: 

1. Mild to moderate hydroureteronephrosis, with narrowing of the contrast
column in the distal ureter compatible with partial obstruction from known
left UVJ stone. Contrast progression into the bladder was seen.

2. Left percutaneous nephrostomy tube placement with pigtail in the renal
pelvis.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of an 8 ___ nephrostomy on the left.

RECOMMENDATION(S):  Routine catheter exchange in 3 months if the nephrostomy
catheter remains in place after lithotripsy.

EXAMINATION:  RENAL U.S.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with history of bilateral perc nephrostomies for
obstructive nephrolithiasis, now with decreased urine output on RIGHT side  //
signs of obstruction of RIGHT kidney / perc nephrostomy

TECHNIQUE:  Grey scale and color Doppler ultrasound images of the kidneys were
obtained.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis ___

FINDINGS: 

The right kidney measures 11.2 cm.  Due to patient discomfort and positioning
the left kidney could not be visualized.  The right kidney shows no
hydronephrosis or mass.  There are several nonobstructing subcentimeter right

There is normal cortical echogenicity and corticomedullary differentiation.

The bladder is moderately well distended and contains a Foley catheter and
several dependent stones, one likely within the left ureterovesicular
junction.

IMPRESSION:


1. Percutaneous nephrostomy within the right renal pelvis without
hydronephrosis.
2. Several nonobstructing stones in the right kidney and urinary bladder.
3. Probable obstructing stone at the left UVJ also seen on recent CT.
4. Due to patient discomfort and positioning the left kidney could not be
visualized.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___, one of your doctors here. You were brought in today because you had a high fever and confusion. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I just remember feeling awful all of a sudden. My sister said I was acting strange.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ve been looking into what’s going on. Your labs showed a high white blood cell count, and your kidney function was a bit off. We did a CT scan and found a kidney stone blocking your left ureter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A kidney stone? But I already have one on the right side with a tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you do. The right nephrostomy is still working fine. But this new stone on the left is causing a backup and infection. That’s why you got so sick—your body was fighting a serious infection from your urine spreading into your blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we caught it early. You were given IV fluids and antibiotics in the ER, and a specialist placed a new tube in your left kidney to relieve the pressure. That’s called a percutaneous nephrostomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So now there are two tubes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one on each side for now. The left one will stay until we can treat the stone. The good news is your vital signs are stabilizing, and your kidney function is already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What kind of infection did I have?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae. It’s a type of bacteria that can cause urinary infections. The good news is it’s sensitive to antibiotics, so we’re treating it effectively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same bug I had before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this is different. You’ve had resistant E. coli and Enterococcus in the past, but this one is responding well to treatment. Infectious disease reviewed your case and we’ve narrowed the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll be on IV antibiotics for a while?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. But if things keep improving, we’ll switch you to a pill form before you go home. You’ll need to finish a full 14-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the tubes? How long will I need them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The right one stays for now since you have chronic stones there. The left one will likely stay until you see your urologist to discuss surgery to remove the stones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? I’ve been putting that off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But with repeated infections and blockages, it might be the best long-term solution. Your urologist will go over the options with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my diet? I’m on ground food and thin liquids, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Because of your swallowing issues, we’re keeping you on ground solids and thin liquids with one-to-one supervision. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood cultures came back negative—no more bacteria growing. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your white count is coming down, and you’re not spiking fevers anymore. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re definitely on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I noticed my left tube is draining pink urine. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a light pink to punch-colored drain is expected after the procedure. As long as there’s no clots or bright red blood, it’s fine. We checked with urology and they agree.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your kidney function is back to normal—creatinine is 0.9. That’s excellent progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. We want to make sure the infection is fully under control. We’ll likely switch you to oral antibiotics tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your third blood culture is negative. We’re going to switch you to ciprofloxacin by mouth today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I won’t need the IV anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for antibiotics. You’ll take cipro twice a day for 14 days. Finish all of it, even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about the urine test that showed yeast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. It’s common with catheters and antibiotics. It’s not causing infection now, so we don’t need to treat it. Just keep an eye out for symptoms like burning or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound today because your right tube wasn’t draining as well. It shows the tube is in place and there’s no blockage on that side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why the low output?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it’s just positioning or clots. The nurse flushed it and it’s draining better now. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Your white count is normal, no fever, and you’re eating well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the cipro for 14 days. Then restart your weekly fosfomycin to prevent future infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tubes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep caring for them as instructed. You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ to discuss surgery. He also wants you to get pulmonary function tests before any procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to call for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the number is on your discharge papers. Call to reschedule—the appointment was missed because of this hospitalization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pressure sores?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re stage II and stable. Continue zinc and vitamin C, and keep shifting positions. Wound care will follow up at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. You’ve improved significantly—mental status clear, vitals stable, infection resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: finish antibiotics, call for PFTs, follow up with urology, and watch for fever or tube issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my sister is picking me up. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve confirmed with her. She’s listed as your contact. Just make sure she knows how to help with the tubes if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s been through this before. We’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over everything one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come a long way. Stay on top of your care and you’ll do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis, neurogenic bladder with a chronic suprapubic catheter, and a history of recurrent drug-resistant urinary tract infections, was admitted for confusion and fever. He was found to have sepsis due to Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteremia originating from an obstructing left ureteral stone causing hydronephrosis. He underwent urgent placement of a left percutaneous nephrostomy for drainage and was started on IV antibiotics. Blood cultures cleared, and he transitioned to oral ciprofloxacin. His condition improved with normalized kidney function and resolution of infection. He was discharged home with instructions to complete a 14-day antibiotic course, restart suppressive fosfomycin therapy, follow up with urology for surgical evaluation of stone burden, and schedule pulmonary function testing prior to any procedure.
